title: The weird world of ‘Diaper Diplomacy’
content:
To unlock more of my reporting on how the internet is reshaping politics, business, media, and culture, and to read my deep dives into emerging online spaces and internet trends, become a paid subscriber today!

I cannot produce this newsletter without your financial support. Your money goes directly towards reporting costs.

Over the past few weeks, YouTube Shorts has become overrun with AI Slop videos, featuring political figures as babies. Diaper Diplomacy, a channel that started just a couple weeks ago has already amassed over 45,000 subscribers and raked in millions of views by uploading AI slop recreations of political debates and political news moments.

These videos are basically boomer bait. The audience who seems to engage with the channel are people who could best be described as Facebook moms and dads. The channel isn’t explicitly right wing, but it’s also not anti Trump. Diaper Diplomacy has recreated, AOC testifying in front of congress and Jasmine Crockett shutting down Marjorie Taylor Green. A recent AI baby recreation of Trump outside Marine One on the White House lawn raked in nearly half a million views.

In addition to being monetized on YouTube, Diaper Diplomacy is funneling users into an AI baby face generating app called Diaper Doppelgänger that costs $9.95 and undoubtedly harvests significant biometric data. The creator is also monetizing through Hulu referral codes on their Linktree.

As more AI content floods the web, I think we'll see more of these strange, anonymously run amorphous channels cropping up in order to capture wide audiences off viral content. Once the page is large enough, if their baby schtick slows down, they can easily flip it to something else or sell it off. These are basically just influence farming operations and AI is making them significantly more pervasive. These types of influence operations are already pervasive on Facebook, but they seem to be a growing plague on YouTube now as well.

I was going on a deep dive into this channel when I read Ryan Broderick and Adam Bumas’ latest piece for Sherwood on how AI-created videos are quietly taking over YouTube. They note that in a profound change from how YouTube looked even just six months ago, four of the top 10 YouTube channels by subscribers in May featured AI-generated material in every video.

From Sherwood:

While not all of the videos from these AI channels are identical, the most successful examples tend to find a theme and stick to it. Some, like “Chick of Honor,” use tools like Hailuo for the instantly established format of cute animals in visibly dangerous or tragic situations. Others, like “Masters of Prophecy,” upload AI-generated music videos for AI-generated songs, made with Suno to evoke ’80s synth nostalgia.

This is a profound change in how YouTube looked even just six months ago. In January, for instance, the most popular account making videos with AI got 2.5 million subscribers and 220 million views — barely in the top 20 for the month. In June, the top four AI channels combined to get more than 23 million subscribers and 800 million views. YouTube’s algorithm clearly favors AI channels now, enough that they’re getting a much better ratio of views to subscriptions.

This does make some sense. Generative-AI-driven channels do fix one core problem YouTube has struggled with ever since it started pushing more professional video content: not every creator has the time, resources, or skills to make Netflix-level content. Google’s ad revenue split doesn’t exactly pay for the costs that come with making your channel more professional, while AI videos all tend to be a certain standard and cost sometimes cents to produce.

Cool project

Internet.flowers is a digital garden made entirely from one woman’s internet browsing history.

Using a Chrome extension she built, every website she visits is scanned and an AI model she trained searches through all the images on those pages to find flowers. When a flower is detected, it is cropped and saved. Over time, all the collected flowers are added to the "garden."

Each flower is quite literally a piece of the artist’s own personal data and, by selling these flowers as bouquets, Mika intentionally leaks and trades her private browsing data. Very creative! 🌸
